(CNN)  -- Two former presidents reflected on their greatest regrets in office Monday, each looking back to issues that continue to plague the nation years later. Former presidents and political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush now share philanthropic efforts. Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana. Asked his biggest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to get Saddam Hussein to leave office at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991. He told the gathering, "I've thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn't do that." But he said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after he was captured has made him reconsider. Bush recalled their talk, "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have." Bush said, "We ended it the way we said we would" as a military success, but noted a cleaner ending "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have been avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him." On a day that President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed the failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians. "My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted. "If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over West Bank then than they do today," Clinton said. "And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors." Clinton said a deal would have helped the U.S. handle other issues in the region, saying, "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that. " Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to "stop the Rwandan genocide," and succeeding on a new health care plan. He said "presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made" with historians, because it teaches lessons. He said he shared problems during the lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, saying, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones." Clinton added, "all of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them aren't right."

Bush and Bill Clinton—once fierce political rivals who now share philanthropic endeavors—reflected on their greatest presidential regrets, contemplating enduring geopolitical issues that continue to challenge the nation today.

When asked about his primary regret after leaving office, Bush revealed that he often ponders whether he should have pressed for Saddam Hussein’s removal at the conclusion of the 1991 Gulf War. Addressing the audience, Bush reflected, “I’ve thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn’t do that.”

However, a conversation with the FBI agent who later interrogated the captured dictator led Bush to reconsider that assumption. Recalling their exchange, Bush said, “I said, ‘What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?’ And this guy said, ‘I’m absolutely convinced he would have.’ My experts tell me he wouldn’t have.” 

While Bush maintained that “we ended it the way we said we would”—achieving a clear military victory—he acknowledged that a more definitive conclusion “would have been perfect.” He added, “If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him.”

Coincidentally, on the same day President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as his special envoy, Clinton addressed his own greatest disappointment: the failure to achieve lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians. 

“My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted,” Clinton stated. He highlighted the momentum of his tenure, noting, “If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over West Bank then than they do today.”

Clinton asserted that a signed agreement would have reshaped the region: “And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors.” 

He further emphasized that resolving the conflict would have significantly enhanced American foreign policy: “We’d be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that.”

In addition to the Middle East, Clinton expressed regret over not doing more to “stop the Rwandan genocide” and failing to enact his administration's healthcare reform plan. Despite these disappointments, he maintained that “presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made” with historians, noting that such transparency imparts vital lessons to successors. 

Recalling a recent luncheon with President Obama and the living former presidents, Clinton remarked, “You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones.” He concluded candidly, “All of us know if you make enough decisions, you’re going to make a few of them aren’t right.”

**Echoes of Unfinished Business: Bush and Clinton Reflect on Foreign Policy Regrets**

In a rare and candid moment of bipartisan statesmanship, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton took the stage together during a joint question-and-answer forum to offer a sweeping retrospective on their time in the Oval Office. While both administrations presided over pivotal triumphs—ranging from the end of the Cold War to a period of unprecedented domestic economic expansion—the discussion turned most poignant when the two leaders were asked to reflect on their greatest executive regrets regarding foreign policy. Their answers revealed the heavy burden of command and illuminated how a few critical crossroads shaped the modern geopolitical landscape.

For George H.W. Bush, the reflection centered on the conclusion of the 1991 Gulf War. Following the swift and decisive victory of Operation Desert Storm, which successfully expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait, President Bush made the strategic decision to stop short of marching to Baghdad to oust Saddam Hussein. At the time, the decision was grounded in diplomatic logic: the United Nations mandate extended only to the liberation of Kuwait, and coalition partners warned against an indefinite occupation. 

However, looking back in hindsight, Bush expressed deep regret over not pressing for Hussein’s complete surrender or removal from power. By leaving the dictator in place, the region suffered another decade of brutal repression, severe humanitarian crises under international sanctions, and ongoing military containment. Bush acknowledged that leaving this "unfinished business" created a volatile vacuum in the Middle East—one that ultimately led to the 2003 invasion of Iraq under his son’s presidency and sparked decades of persistent regional instability.

Bill Clinton’s most haunting foreign policy regret lay not in a war uncompleted, but in a peace unmade. Clinton reflected extensively on his exhaustive, late-career push to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, culminating in the historic 2000 Camp David Summit. Clinton had brought Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat together, investing immense personal capital to broker a definitive two-state solution. 

With visible emotion, Clinton lamented his failure to secure a final peace agreement, pointing specifically to Yasser Arafat’s ultimate unwillingness to accept the compromised terms on the table. Clinton recalled the tragic turn of events that followed: the collapse of the negotiations was swiftly succeeded by the outbreak of the Second Intifada, a devastating wave of violence that shattered the trust between Israelis and Palestinians. Clinton reflected that missing that narrow window of opportunity doomed the region to renewed cycles of conflict, extremist violence, and an increasingly elusive prospect for peace that continues to trouble global security today.

Together, the reflections of Bush and Clinton offered a sobering masterclass in the unintended consequences of high-stakes presidential diplomacy. Whether through military restraint that left a tyrant in power or diplomatic efforts that fell just short of a historic breakthrough, both former commanders-in-chief underscored the agonizing limits of American executive power. Their joint exchange served as a powerful reminder to current and future leaders that the decisions made—or missed—in the heat of global crises cast long, defining shadows over the stability of the world for generations to come.

**NEW ORLEANS (CNN)** — In an extraordinary display of bipartisan unity and candor, former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush took the stage together in New Orleans on Thursday to reflect on the highest office in the land—and the decisions that still haunt them.

Speaking at a leadership forum hosted by Tulane University, the former political rivals, who forged a famous post-presidential friendship while co-leading Hurricane Katrina relief efforts, offered a packed audience a rare glimpse into the heavy burdens of the commander-in-chief.

For Clinton, the conversation turned quickly to foreign policy and the human cost of inaction. He identified his administration’s failure to intervene during the 1994 Rwandan genocide as his single greatest presidential regret.

"We didn’t act fast enough, and hundreds of thousands of lives were lost," Clinton told the audience, his voice dropping. "It was a failure of the international community, but as president, it was my failure. I have to live with that every day. Power is meaningless if you don't use it when humanity needs it most."

Bush, the nation’s 41st president, looked inward at both domestic politics and the personal toll of leadership. He pointed to his broken 1988 campaign promise—“Read my lips: no new taxes”—which he eventually abandoned in a 1990 budget deal with Congressional Democrats to curb a growing deficit.

"Breaking that pledge cost me politically, and it damaged the trust people placed in me," Bush admitted with characteristic self-deprecation. "You make what you believe is the right compromise for the country’s balance sheet, but in politics, compromises carry a heavy price. It contributed to me sitting next to Bill as a one-term president," he added, drawing laughter from the crowd.

Bush also spoke somberly about the weight of sending young Americans into combat during the 1991 Gulf War. "Writing those letters to the families of fallen soldiers... that never leaves you," he said.

Despite the heavy subject matter, the event highlighted the deep, unlikely bond between the two men who once fought bitterly for the White House in 1992. Throughout the evening, the pair traded lighthearted banter about their golf games and their post-presidential lives, modeling a civil political dialogue that both lamented is increasingly rare today.

As the forum drew to a close, both men offered advice to future generations of public servants, emphasizing that mistakes are an inevitable part of governance.

"The presidency isn't about being perfect," Bush noted. "It's about making the tough calls with the best information you have, and having the humility to learn when you fall short."

Clinton echoed the sentiment, looking at his former adversary with a smile. "George and I disagreed on plenty," Clinton said. "But at the end of the day, you have to remember that we’re all on the same team. I only wish we’d figured that out a little sooner."

**SAN FRANCISCO** — Setting aside the bitter political rivalry that defined the 1992 presidential campaign, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton took the stage together at the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA) annual convention, offering a crowd of thousands a rare, candid glimpse into the burdens of the commander-in-chief.

Speaking before an audience of auto executives and dealers, the 41st and 42nd presidents demonstrated a warm, easy camaraderie that has increasingly characterized their post-presidential relationship. Yet the central focus of their joint appearance turned serious as both men reflected on the shadow of unfulfilled goals and foreign policy miscalculations that marked their respective administrations.

For former President Bush, the discussion turned to the aftermath of the 1991 Gulf War. While Operation Desert Storm was hailed as a tactical victory that successfully expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait, Bush addressed the long-standing criticism surrounding his decision to cease hostilities without removing Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein from power.

Bush defended the diplomatic constraints of the international coalition he assembled, but openly admitted to a key miscalculation regarding Hussein’s resilience.

"I miscalculated on one fundamental point—I genuinely believed the Iraqi military or the Iraqi people would move to oust Saddam after such a devastating and decisive defeat," Bush told the audience. "Our mandate from the United Nations was clear: liberate Kuwait, not occupy Baghdad. But leaving him in power proved to be a persistent thorn in the side of the international community, and it remains one of the great frustrations of my presidency."

The 41st president noted that while he stood by the strategic decision not to overextend American forces into Baghdad, the lingering threat posed by Hussein was an agonizing unresolved issue. 

Taking the microphone, Clinton offered his own stark assessment of what he considered his greatest foreign policy disappointment: the failure to secure a lasting peace agreement between Israelis and Palestinians during the final months of his second term. 

Clinton reflected intensely on the July 2000 Camp David Summit, where he brought Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Palestinian Authority Chairman Yasser Arafat together for high-stakes negotiations. Despite historic concessions offered by the Israeli delegation, the talks ultimately collapsed, followed shortly by the outbreak of the Second Intifada.

Clinton placed the blame squarely on Arafat’s refusal to accept the proposed peace framework, which would have established an independent Palestinian state.

"I worked night and day for eight years, right up until my last hour in office, to try to achieve peace in the Middle East," Clinton said. "We got closer than anyone ever had. Prime Minister Barak was willing to make monumental compromises, but Yasser Arafat simply could not make the final leap from being a revolutionary to being a statesman."

Clinton recalled a poignant moment from the end of his term, emphasizing the magnitude of the missed opportunity.

"Arafat called me a few days before I left office and told me I was a great man," Clinton recounted, his voice dropping. "I told him, 'I am not a great man. I am a failure, and you made me one.' He missed a historic chance to give his people a sovereign nation with a capital in East Jerusalem, and that failure breaks my heart to this day."

Despite the heavy subject matter, the tone between the two former presidents remained deeply respectful, illustrating a striking evolution from their fierce campaign battles a decade earlier. The joint appearance highlighted a growing tradition of post-presidential diplomacy and friendship, with both leaders acknowledging that the perspective gained after leaving the Oval Office often reveals the shared challenges inherent to the presidency.

For the attendees at the NADA convention, the session offered more than political nostalgia; it provided an unvarnished masterclass in the complexities of global leadership from two men who once held the weight of the world on their shoulders.

**CNN SPECIAL REPORT**

**HEADLINE:** SHARED BURDENS: Clinton and Bush 41 Reflect on Their Biggest Presidential Regrets in Joint Louisiana Appearance

**DATELINE:** NEW ORLEANS, Louisiana (CNN) — 

In a rare and candid display of bipartisan reflection, former political rivals President Bill Clinton and President George H.W. Bush took the stage together in Louisiana, offering a striking look into the burdens of the Oval Office. 

The two former chief executives—who teamed up in the wake of Hurricane Katrina to lead bipartisan fundraising efforts for Gulf Coast relief—put aside past political battles to discuss the personal and political decisions that continue to haunt them years after leaving office.

Here are the main presidential regrets expressed by the 41st and 42nd presidents during their joint appearance.

---

### **Bill Clinton: Foreign Inaction and Domestic Stalls**

For Bill Clinton, the conversation centered largely on the moral weight of inaction during his two terms, particularly regarding international humanitarian crises.

*   **The Rwanda Genocide (1994):** Clinton reiterated that his single biggest regret as commander-in-chief was the U.S. failure to intervene during the 1994 Rwandan genocide, where an estimated 800,000 people were killed in roughly 100 days. Clinton acknowledged that a prompt international response—even deploying a modest military force—could have saved hundreds of thousands of lives. 
*   **Health Care Reform:** On the domestic front, Clinton expressed deep regret over the collapse of his 1993–1994 health care reform initiative. He conceded that overplaying his hand and failing to build a workable bipartisan consensus doomed what he considered one of his most vital policy goals.
*   **National Security Constraints:** Clinton also touched upon the frustration of not neutralizing Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda before leaving office, despite authorizing strikes and covert operations in the late 1990s.

---

### **George H.W. Bush: Broken Pledges and Communication Gaps**

George H.W. Bush reflected on the political decisions that fractured his coalition and ultimately cost him a second term in the 1992 election against Clinton.

*   **"Read My Lips":** Bush admitted that his biggest political regret was breaking his famous 1988 campaign promise: *"Read my lips: no new taxes."* Facing a massive federal deficit in 1990, Bush agreed to a compromise budget deal with Congressional Democrats that included tax increases. While maintaining it was the responsible thing to do for the nation's long-term fiscal health, he conceded it was a fatal political error that alienated his conservative base.
*   **Failing to Connect on the Economy:** The 41st president expressed regret over how his administration communicated with the public during the economic downturn of the early 1990s. He admitted that he failed to adequately convey his empathy for struggling Americans, allowing the narrative to take hold that he was out of touch with everyday economic anxieties.
*   **Post-Gulf War Aftermath:** While defending the decision to stop the 1991 Gulf War after liberating Kuwait rather than pushing on to Baghdad, Bush expressed lingering sadness over the immediate fallout—specifically the brutal suppression of the Marsh Arabs and Kurds by Saddam Hussein’s regime following the war.

---

### **A Shared Weight: The Human Cost of War**

Beyond specific policy decisions, both former presidents agreed on the single heaviest burden of the presidency: sending young American service members into harm’s way. 

Bush and Clinton described the agonizing process of writing letters of condolence to the families of fallen soldiers, agreeing that no amount of political success could ease the emotional toll of those losses.

---

### **THE CNN BOTTOM LINE**

`[CNN GRAPHIC: FROM RIVALS TO RECOVERY PARTNERS]`

What began as a bitter fight for the presidency in 1992 has evolved into one of the most remarkable friendships in modern American political history. As they stood together in storm-damaged Louisiana, Clinton and Bush offered a stark reminder that while political legacies are shaped by triumphs, they are often defined by the heavy weight of regret. 

*Reporting live from New Orleans, this is CNN.*

**CNN Headline:** Rivals turned allies: Clinton and Bush Sr. reflect on presidential regrets, offer advice to Obama at New Orleans event

**By [Author Name], CNN**

**NEW ORLEANS (CNN)** — In a rare and candid joint appearance, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton took the stage in New Orleans on Thursday, offering a reflective look at their time in the White House, detailing their biggest political regrets, and sharing the counsel they have passed along to President Barack Obama.

Despite their bitter battle for the presidency in 1992, the two elder statesmen displayed the warm, bipartisan friendship that has defined their post-presidential years. Speaking before a packed audience, the former commanders-in-chief engaged in an uncommonly frank discussion about the burdens of the Oval Office and the clarity that comes with hindsight.

### Bush on the Gulf War and Saddam Hussein

Reflecting on his single term in office, Bush addressed one of the most scrutinised foreign policy decisions of his presidency: the conclusion of the 1991 Gulf War. 

While defending the decision to limit the U.S.-led coalition’s mandate to liberating Kuwait rather than marching to Baghdad, Bush acknowledged the lingering questions over leaving Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein in power. 

"You always look back and wonder if you could have done things differently," Bush said. He noted the agonizing balance between achieving a clearly defined military objective and predicting the long-term regional consequences, admitting that Saddam’s continued survival in power remained a complex shadow over the victory.

### Clinton on Rwanda, Middle East Peace, and Healthcare

Clinton was equally unreserved about the missteps of his eight years in office, identifying the 1994 Rwandan genocide as the single greatest failure of his administration. 

"Not acting faster in Rwanda is something I live with every day," Clinton confessed, stating that the international community’s inaction during the crisis remains his deepest regret.

Turning to the Middle East, Clinton reflected on the intense, late-term push for a two-state solution at the 2000 Camp David Summit. He expressed lingering frustration over the failure to secure a breakthrough between Israeli and Palestinian leaders, noting that despite coming excruciatingly close, the inability to seal a peace agreement with Yasser Arafat remains a painful missed opportunity.

On the domestic front, Clinton pointed to his administration’s failed 1993 healthcare reform effort. He admitted to political overreach and tactical errors, acknowledging that the aggressive push—without adequate bipartisan buy-in—ultimately set back the cause of healthcare reform for years and cost Democrats control of Congress in 1994.

### Counsel for President Obama

The conversation shifted to the current occupant of the Oval Office, President Barack Obama, who has frequently sought the advice of his predecessors amidst economic recovery efforts and ongoing foreign conflicts.

Both men emphasized that the extreme isolation of the presidency creates a unique fraternity among those who have held the job. 

Bush shared that his primary advice to Obama has been to "tune out the noise" and trust his core instincts when making life-and-death decisions, noting that a president cannot govern by daily opinion polls.

Clinton revealed that his counsel to Obama focused heavily on Washington mechanics, advising the president to invest heavily in building personal relationships on Capitol Hill, even with political opponents. 

"You can’t govern a country as big and diverse as America from an island," Clinton said. "You have to bring people into the room who disagree with you, and you have to keep talking."

### A Lasting Legacy

The New Orleans event highlighted the unique partnership the two men forged long after their electoral clash—a bond originally cemented when they co-chaired national fundraising efforts following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

As the event drew to a close, both former presidents agreed that while history ultimately sits in judgment of any administration, the weight of unfulfilled promises and strategic errors is a burden every chief executive carries long after leaving the White House.

counterfactuals.prompt: Pretend you are a reporter for CNN covering an event where former presidents Bush Sr. and Clinton talk about what they wish they'd done differently while in office. Can you write a brief article with their quotes on foreign policy and learning from past mistakes?
counterfactuals.output:
**COLLEGE STATION, Texas (CNN)** — In a rare and candid moment of bipartisan reflection, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton took the stage together at the George Bush Presidential Library on Thursday, offering an intimate look at the foreign policy decisions that defined their presidencies—and the lessons learned from the ones they got wrong.

Despite having been fierce rivals in the 1992 presidential campaign, the 41st and 42nd presidents demonstrated the deep post-presidential friendship they have forged in recent years, united by the unique burden of leading the free world through rapid global transformation.

Opening the discussion on foreign policy, Bush reflected on his administration’s navigation of the end of the Cold War and the 1991 Gulf War. While widely praised for building an international coalition during Operation Desert Storm, the former president admitted that managing the aftermath of conflicts was an area where he wished his team had taken a different approach.

"Foreign policy is about managing the crises you didn't see coming, but it's also about anticipating the dust that settles after the storm," Bush said. "Looking back, particularly in the Middle East after Desert Storm, I wish we had done a better job of communicating our long-term intent to the region and anticipating the political vacuum that remained. You learn very quickly in that office that solving one complex problem often plants the seeds for the next."

Bush noted that his biggest takeaway was the importance of restraint balanced with clear diplomacy. "The mistake is thinking victory on the battlefield automatically translates to peace on the ground. It requires just as much work after the shooting stops."

Succeeding Bush in 1993, Clinton inherited a shifting geopolitical landscape. During the panel, he spoke openly about the limitations of U.S. power and pointed directly to what he considers the greatest failure of his two terms in office: the international community's failure to stop the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

"If I could turn back the clock, the speed and scale of our response to Rwanda is my single biggest regret," Clinton said, his voice quiet. "We were still reeling from the fallout of our mission in Somalia, and that caution proved fatal. We let the fear of getting bogged down paralyze us when hundreds of thousands of innocent lives were on the line."

Clinton emphasized that his hard-learned lesson from Rwanda later shaped his administration's decisive intervention in Kosovo in 1999. 

"The hardest lesson I had to learn is that early action, even when politically risky, is almost always less costly than late action," Clinton added. "The fear of making a mistake can sometimes lead to a far worse outcome: inaction."

Both former commanders-in-chief agreed that no president leaves office with a perfect foreign policy record, pointing out that intelligence is rarely complete and the consequences of presidential orders are felt for generations.

Closing the event, Bush offered a piece of advice for future occupants of the Oval Office. 

"You make the best call you can with the information you have," Bush said, looking over at Clinton. "But humility—knowing that you don't have all the answers and being willing to adjust when you're wrong—is the most important asset a foreign policy team can have."
